title: Blood on the Snow
text:
Once upon a time there was a Queen who was out driving in her sleigh. It was winter, and fresh snow had just fallen. She hadn’t gone far when her nose began to bleed, and she had to climb out. She stood by the fence with the horses steaming behind her, looking at the red blood on the white snow, and it came into her mind that she had twelve sons and not a single daughter.

“If only I had a daughter as white as snow and as red as blood,” she said to herself, “I wouldn’t care what became of my sons.”

The words were hardly out of her mouth before a troll-wife stood at her elbow, leaning in close.

“A daughter you shall have,” said the troll-wife, “and she shall be as white as snow and as red as blood. But then your sons shall be mine. You may keep them until the child is christened.”

When her time came, the Queen gave birth to a daughter, and she was as white as snow and as red as blood, just as the troll-wife had promised. So they named her Snow-White and Rose-Red. There was great rejoicing at the King’s manor, and the Queen was happier than words could say. But then she remembered her promise. She sent for a silversmith and had him make twelve silver spoons, one for each prince. Then she had him make one more, exactly like the others, and that one she gave to Snow-White and Rose-Red.

The moment the princess had been christened, the twelve princes turned into twelve wild ducks and flew away. Nobody saw them again. They were gone, and gone they stayed.

The princess grew up tall and lovely. But there was often something strange and sorrowful about her, and nobody could make out what ailed her.

Then one evening the Queen was sorrowful too, for no doubt her mind ran on strange things whenever she thought of her sons.

“Why are you so sad, my child?” she asked Snow-White and Rose-Red. “If something’s troubling you, tell me. If there’s anything you want, you shall have it.”

“Oh, it’s so lonely,” said Snow-White and Rose-Red. “Everyone else has brothers and sisters. I have nobody. That’s what I grieve for.”

“You had brothers too, my child,” said the Queen. “I had twelve sons, and they were your brothers. But I gave them all away to have you.”

And she told her the whole story.

From that day on the princess had no peace. She would go, and she had to go, to find her brothers, for it seemed to her that all of it was her fault. The Queen wept and pleaded, but it was no use. In the end the princess left the manor. She walked and she walked, so far out into the wide world that you would never believe so fine a young lady could have walked so far.

Once she had been walking a long time in a great, great forest. She grew tired, sat down on a tussock and fell asleep. She dreamed that she went deeper into the forest and came to a little log cabin, and there were her brothers. At that she woke, and right in front of her was a path trodden into the green moss, leading in among the trees. She followed it, and at long last she came to a little log cabin, just like the one in her dream.

There was nobody home. But in the main room stood twelve beds and twelve chairs, and on the table lay twelve silver spoons, just like the one in her pocket. There were twelve of everything. She was happier than she had been for years, for now she knew that this was where her brothers lived.

She lit the fire, swept the floor, made the beds and cooked a meal, and she tidied and prettied the place as best she could. When everything was ready, she ate a little herself. But she left her spoon lying on the table. Then she crept under the youngest brother’s bed and lay still.

She had hardly lain down when there came a rushing and a whistling in the air, and in flew all twelve wild ducks. But the moment they were over the threshold, they turned into princes.
imagePrompt: In a silent winter lane beside a wooden fence, the Queen has stepped down from her sleigh and stares at bright red blood dripping onto fresh white snow; behind her, a troll-wife—an uncanny, otherworldly bargain-maker wrapped in dark, ragged finery—has appeared as if from the cold air, leaning close to speak her promise, while the horses steam in the frost and the pale sky hangs heavy with snow.

title: The Silent Girl on the Bog
text:
“Oh, how warm and snug it is in here!” they said. “God bless whoever lit the fire and cooked us such good food!”

Each of them took his silver spoon and was about to eat. But when every one of them had taken his own, there was still a spoon lying on the table, and it was so like the others that nobody could tell them apart. They looked at the spoon, and they looked at one another.

“That’s our sister’s spoon,” they said. “And if her spoon is here, she can’t be far away.”

“If that’s our sister’s spoon, and she’s here, then she must die,” said the eldest. “She’s to blame for all our misery.”

And she lay under the bed and heard every word.

“No,” said the youngest. “It would be a sin to kill her for that. It’s not her fault we suffer. If anyone’s to blame, it’s our own mother.”

So they searched for her high and low, and at last they looked under the beds. Under the youngest brother’s bed they found her, and they dragged her out.

The eldest still wanted her killed, but she wept and begged so sweetly for her life.

“Oh, dear Lord, don’t kill me!” she said. “I’ve walked for years and years looking for you. If I could save you, I’d gladly give my life.”

“If you’ll save us, you may live,” they said. “For if you’re willing, you can.”

“Just tell me how,” said the princess, “and I’ll do it, whatever it is.”

“You must gather bog-cotton,” said the princes, “and card it and spin it and weave it into cloth. Out of the cloth you must cut and sew twelve caps, twelve shirts and twelve kerchiefs, one set for each of us. And while you’re doing it, you must neither speak nor laugh nor weep. If you can do that, we’re saved.”

“But where will I find bog-cotton enough for so many caps and shirts and kerchiefs?” asked Snow-White and Rose-Red.

“We’ll show you,” said the princes.

Before dawn the next morning they took her out to a great, great bog. The bog-cotton grew so thick there that there wasn’t room for one tuft more, and it nodded in the wind. When the sun came up over the ridge, every tuft caught the light, and the whole bog shone white as snow as far as the eye could see. The princess had never seen so much bog-cotton in all her life.

The brothers stood around her in a half-circle. The eldest handed her a sack and pointed out across the bog. The youngest said nothing. He only looked at her. She held the sack tight and nodded. She didn’t say a word. And it would be many years before she said another.

Then the sun was up, and where a moment ago she had had twelve brothers, twelve wild ducks rose from the bog.

So it went on, well and long. By day she gathered bog-cotton, and when it grew dark she carded and spun. She wove, and she cut, and she sewed, and in between she kept house for her brothers: she cooked their food and made their beds. In the evening they came rushing and whirring home as wild ducks. At night they were princes. In the morning they flew off again and were wild ducks all day long.

But then one day, when she was out on the bog gathering bog-cotton—and if I’m not mistaken, it was the last time she needed to go—the young King who ruled that land came riding by on a hunt. He saw her standing knee-deep among the reeds with her arms full of bog-cotton, and he reined in his horse. Who could this lovely girl be, wading about the bog all by herself? So he asked her. But he got no answer, and that made him wonder all the more. His horse pawed at the wet ground while he sat there looking at her, and he liked her so much that he wanted to take her home to his manor and marry her.
imagePrompt: In a vast sunlit bog where bog-cotton gleams like scattered snow, Snow-White and Rose-Red—a princess as white as snow and as red as blood—stands knee-deep among reeds, silently gathering fluffy white tufts into her arms; at the bog’s edge the Young King, dressed for the hunt and holding his reins, has ridden up and watches her with astonished curiosity, his horse pawing at the wet ground.

title: Ducks Over the Pyre
text:
So he told his men to lift her up onto his horse. Snow-White and Rose-Red wrung her hands and made signs and pointed at the sacks that held all her work, and when the King understood that she wanted them with her, he told his men to bring the sacks as well. Little by little she came round to it, for the King was a kind man and a handsome one, and he was as gentle with her as anyone could be.

But when they reached the manor, the King’s stepmother, the old Queen, set eyes on Snow-White and Rose-Red. The girl was so beautiful that the old Queen was sick with anger and jealousy, and she went straight to the King.

“Can’t you see that this girl you’ve brought home and want to marry is a witch?” she said. “She neither speaks nor laughs nor weeps.”

The King paid her no heed. He married Snow-White and Rose-Red, and they lived in great joy and splendour. But she didn’t forget the shirts for all that. She sewed on them every single day.

Before the year was out, the young Queen had a little prince, and that made the old Queen angrier and more jealous than ever. Late in the night she crept in to the young Queen while she slept, took the baby and threw it into the snake pit. Then she cut the young Queen’s finger, smeared the blood around her mouth and went to the King.

“Come and see what kind of queen you’ve married,” she said. “She’s eaten her own child.”

Snow-White and Rose-Red said nothing. She couldn’t.

The King was so heartsick that he nearly wept.

“Well, it must be true, since I see it with my own eyes,” he said. “But surely she won’t do it again. This time I’ll spare her.”

Before the year was out, she had another son, and it went exactly the same way. The old Queen crept in by night, took the baby and threw it into the snake pit, cut the young Queen’s finger and smeared the blood around her mouth. Then she told the King that his wife had eaten this child too. The King was so grief-stricken you would never believe it.

“Well, it must be true, since I see it with my own eyes,” he said. “But surely she won’t do it again. I’ll spare her this time too.”

Before the year was out, Snow-White and Rose-Red had a daughter, and the old Queen took her as well and threw her into the snake pit. While the young Queen slept, the old Queen cut her finger and smeared the blood around her mouth, and then she went to the King.

“Now come and see if it isn’t just as I’ve told you,” she said. “She’s a troll-witch. Now she’s eaten her third child as well.”

Then the King’s grief knew no bounds. He could spare her no longer. He had to give orders for her to be burned alive on a pyre.

When the pyre was blazing and they were about to put her on it, she made signs to them to fetch twelve boards and lay them in a ring around the fire. Then she knelt and laid out the caps and the shirts and the kerchiefs for her brothers, a set on every board. But the youngest brother’s shirt had no left sleeve. She hadn’t had time to finish it.

No sooner had she done this than there came a rushing and a roaring in the air, and twelve wild ducks came flying over the forest. They swooped down through the smoke and sparks, and each of them snatched up its clothes in its beak and flew off with them.

The old Queen stood beside the King, and she pointed.

“Now do you see?” she said. “Now you can see for yourself she’s a witch! Hurry up and burn her before the wood burns out!”

The King looked at the fire, and at his wife, and at the sky where the ducks had gone.

“Oh, we’ve wood enough,” he said. “We’ve the whole forest to take from. I’ll wait a little. I’d like to see how this ends.”
imagePrompt: Before a roaring pyre in the palace yard, Snow-White and Rose-Red, still silent and pale-faced yet resolute, kneels beside twelve boards laid around the flames and places bog-cotton garments—caps, shirts, and cloth—neatly upon them, one shirt missing a left sleeve; overhead, twelve wild ducks burst through smoke and sparks, each seizing a garment in its beak as the Old Queen (the jealous stepmother) points accusingly and the Young King looks on, torn between horror and doubt.

title: The Children in the Snake Pit
text:
At that very moment twelve princes came riding up, as tall and handsome as you could wish to see. But the youngest had a duck’s wing where his left arm should have been.

“What’s going on here?” asked the princes.

“My Queen is to be burned,” said the King, “because she’s a witch and has eaten her own children.”

“She hasn’t eaten her children,” said the princes. “Speak now, sister! You’ve saved us. Now save yourself!”

Then Snow-White and Rose-Red spoke. She told them how it had all come about: how each time she had given birth, the old Queen, the King’s stepmother, had crept in to her in the night, taken the baby, cut her finger and smeared the blood around her mouth. And as she spoke, she wept. She was allowed to now.

The princes took the King and led him to the snake pit, and everyone followed. The snake pit was an old walled yard of stone behind the manor, dank and dim and crawling with snakes and toads. And there lay the three children, playing with the snakes and the toads, and lovelier children you never saw in all your days.

The King picked them up and carried them over to his stepmother.

“What punishment,” he asked, “does someone deserve who could find it in her heart to betray an innocent queen and three such blessed children?”

“She should be bound between twelve wild horses,” said the old Queen, “so that each of them takes its share.”

“You have spoken your own sentence,” said the King, “and you shall suffer it.”

So the old Queen was bound between twelve wild horses, and each of them took its share.

But Snow-White and Rose-Red took the King and her children and her twelve brothers, and they went home to her mother and father and told them everything that had happened. And there was joy and gladness throughout the kingdom, because the princess was saved, and she had saved her twelve brothers too.
imagePrompt: Inside a grim stone snake-yard, the Twelve Princes—handsome and newly restored, the youngest marked by a duck’s wing where his left arm should be—stand with the Young King as they look down in disbelief at three small royal children alive and playing fearlessly among coiling snakes and squat toads; the children’s bright faces and clean clothes contrast with the damp, shadowed stones and tangled creatures at their feet.
